text: This is an illustrative scenario, not a real company or a real incident -- but the mistake it demonstrates is common and well documented in security automation. Caldera Finance built an automated containment script without a dry-run default, a blast-radius cap, or a human approval gate, to resolve one real compromised account as fast as possible.

Their correlation query looked for any account signing in from the same IP as the compromised one, within the active incident's time window. That query was syntactically correct. The mistake was upstream: the IP it matched against wasn't the attacker's address, it was the corporate VPN's shared exit IP, which thirty-eight other employees were also routing through that same afternoon for entirely unrelated, legitimate work.

The automation rule fired and disabled all thirty-nine matching accounts, not because the script threw an error, but because it did exactly what it was told against a signal that meant something different than the person who wrote the rule assumed. Thirty-eight employees were locked out mid-shift with no warning.

The real incident got slower to resolve, not faster. The same SOC team investigating the actual compromise spent the next two hours fielding confused help-desk tickets and manually re-enabling thirty-eight unrelated accounts instead of focusing on the one that mattered.

Three separate guardrails each would have caught this alone. A dry-run default would have logged would disable 39 accounts, an obviously wrong number for the first human who saw it. A hard blast-radius cap of one account per action would have made the bad query harmless. And the approval gate from Lesson 29's execute_containment -- a human asking why thirty-nine -- would have caught the shared-IP mistake in seconds.

None of those three guardrails fixes the underlying query. All three stop a bad query from causing real damage anyway. Good automation doesn't depend on every correlation rule being written perfectly the first time -- it depends on a wrong rule failing safely instead of failing wide, which is exactly what Lesson 32 pulls together across this whole course.
